ask: The project text says to report “all five metrics from Section 4”, but that section only lists three: ROC-AUC, PR-AUC and F1. We report six (those three plus precision, recall and accuracy). Is that fine, or did you have five specific metrics in mind?
why: We already compute all six, so this only decides what we show in the results table and plots.

ask: We compare four models: a baseline, logistic regression, a random forest and a neural network. We use SHAP and LIME on the random forest, but our prediction function uses the neural network (it scored best on the validation data, although the forest is almost tied). Is it okay to explain a different model from the one the prediction function uses, or should they be the same model?
why: SHAP is exact and simple for a random forest, which is how Lab 4 does it. Explaining the neural network would need extra tools the labs don't cover. If you want the same model in both places, we would either explain the network or use the forest in the prediction function.

ask: The project text says each row is “one driver entering one race”. We only keep drivers who actually started the race, so drivers who entered but never started (didn't qualify, withdrew) are dropped. Is that okay, or should they stay in the data as “no podium”?
why: About 1,640 of the 26,670 rows (6%) are drivers who never started. Keeping them would lower the podium rate and count cars that never raced.

ask: The project text asks for permutation importance, but our lab manuals and guide notebooks only teach SHAP and LIME. We wrote permutation importance ourselves: shuffle one input column, score the model again, and see how much worse it gets. Is that fine, and how much detail do you want when we explain it?
why: We checked all four lab manuals and the three guide notebooks and none of them mentions it. We wrote it by hand because the scikit-learn version doesn't work with our neural network.

ask: How we choose features: we start with just the starting grid, then add one group of related features at a time (for example all the driver-standings features) and keep a group only if the validation score improves. Afterwards we run the ablation: we take each group out of the finished model and see how much worse it gets. Is that the order you expect (choose first, then use the ablation to measure each group), or should the ablation be what decides which features we keep?
why: The project text says features are justified before training and the ablation measures their contribution afterwards, so we read them as two separate steps. If the ablation had to do the choosing it wouldn't work well here: with all 11 features, taking out any single group barely changes the score, because the groups overlap.

ask: For the ablation, is it enough to take out the groups of our final features (starting grid and driver standings) for each model, or do you also want every candidate group removed? And should we show the results on the validation data, the test data, or both?
why: Right now we do all of it: the final features for all three models, and all 11 candidates for logistic regression and the forest, shown on validation and test. We only want to know whether that is more than needed. The test results are never used to make a decision.

ask: The checklist asks for a “form” feature: how well a driver or team has done in its last few races. We use the share of the last 5 races that ended on the podium, using only past races. We built it and checked there is no leakage, but it didn't make the models better, so it isn't in our final features. Is that fine?
why: We would rather not force a feature in just to tick a box. The code, the leakage check and the test of whether it helps are all in the notebook.

ask: You said to show each attempt in its own cell or section, so the before and after is visible. For choosing features we try all the options in one loop and show one table with a row per attempt (the hyperparameter search works the same way). Is a table like that enough, or do you want every attempt as a separate cell?
why: Separate cells would make the notebook a lot longer. The table shows every attempt with its score, so nothing is hidden, but we want to be sure that counts.

ask: The checklist asks for the “effect of the step on data distribution, range and values”. We show before and after for the cleaning steps, for filling in missing values and for scaling. Is that enough, or do you want it for every step, including the ones that build the features?
why: Showing it for every step would add many plots, so we want to know where to stop.

ask: Our baseline is a logistic regression that only uses the starting grid. The other models score about 0.06 to 0.07 higher on our main metric (PR-AUC about 0.71 to 0.73, against 0.65 to 0.67 for the baseline). Is that a good enough baseline, and is that the size of improvement you would expect?
why: The starting grid already explains a lot of who finishes on the podium, so there isn't much room left to improve.

ask: For the mechanical-retirement question, we count any retirement that isn't clearly a crash, a driver problem or a rule decision as mechanical. That includes vague reasons like “Retired” or “Puncture” (about a fifth of the cases we count). Is that okay if we explain the rule, or should we leave the unclear ones out?
why: We checked it both ways. Leaving the unclear ones out lowers the rates (11.2% to 9.0%, and 6.9% to 5.5%), but cars still got more reliable, so the answer doesn't change.

ask: We use a few things the labs didn't teach, for example confidence intervals for the rates, joining tables with pandas, and a bootstrap test for the preprocessing experiments. Is that fine as long as we can explain each one and why we used it?
why: The full list is in our out-of-scope file. We would rather not drop useful methods, but we want to know what you expect.

ask: In the evaluation, how deep should our explanations go: the idea in simple words, or the maths as well (for example how SHAP values are calculated, or how a neural network learns)?
why: This decides how much of the extra material we need to study in depth.

ask: Our notebook starts with a line that installs three packages (shap, lime and missingno), so the internet has to be switched on, for example on Kaggle. Is that okay, and is there a time limit for running the notebook? A full run takes about 14 minutes.
why: If the notebook is run somewhere without internet that first line fails, so we want to know what you expect.

ask: Do you expect the report to follow a specific structure or length? And does every plot in the notebook also have to be in the report?
why: The project text says the plots and answers must be in both. Our report has all 26 figures and the three answers; we just want to be sure we aren't missing a required format.
